title: CAN WE BELIEVE OUR OWN EYES?

source.filename: Practice 119 - IETLS 閱讀練習 - Passage 2.pdf

paragraphs.text: Can We Believe Our Own Eyes? 1. An optical illusion is a visually perceived image that is deceptive or misleading because information transmitted from the eye to the brain is processed in such a way that the resulting assumption or deduction does not represent physical reality. Our perception of what we see can be influenced by several external factors. Illusions fall into two main categories: physiological illusions and cognitive illusions. Cognitive illusions can be divided into four subtypes.

Physiological illusions result from excessive stimulation of the eyes and brain, which creates a temporary state of confusion and mixed messages. After exposure to extremely vivid light, for example, the eyes may need time to adapt, and we may briefly see things that are not normally present. In the same way, a contingent perceptual after-effect may occur after someone stares at a particular colour: receptors in the brain may process subsequent colours inaccurately until the overload has passed.

Cognitive illusions, on the other hand, are said to arise not from neurone activity but from assumptions we consciously make based on our knowledge and experience of the world. The four categories are ambiguous, distorting, paradox and fictional illusions. Including fictional illusions in the cognitive group is somewhat misleading, however, because this type is seen only by an individual in a particular situation and has no tangible form. A fictional illusion is, in fact, a hallucination caused by drug use or a brain condition such as schizophrenia.

Ambiguous illusions are pictures or objects structured so that their form can be perceived in more than one way. One individual may perceive an image differently from another, and the same person can often interpret it in more than one form. A classic example is the Necker cube, a standard line drawing that our visual system generally interprets as a three-dimensional box. Where the lines cross, the drawing deliberately does not define which line is in front and which is behind. The mind nevertheless interprets what it sees. Because people generally view objects from above, most interpret the cube’s lower-left face as the front, with the base of that face parallel to the floor. It is also possible, however, to interpret a different face as the front.

The Necker cube contributed to researchers’ understanding of the human visual system by providing evidence that the brain is a neural network with two distinct, interchangeable states. It has also been used in epistemology—the study of knowledge—to challenge direct realism, the theory that the world is exactly as the human mind perceives it. With the Necker cube, we can generally see either or both versions of a three-dimensional cube even though the image is only a two-dimensional drawing made up of 12 lines.

Distorting illusions affect a person’s ability to judge size, length or curvature. The Müller-Lyer illusion, which consists of three lines with arrow-like ends, is a prime example. The middle line has two outward-pointing ends, the line above it has two inward-pointing ends, and the third has one of each. Many respondents from certain backgrounds say that the middle line is the longest, although all three are equal. Cultural background affects perceptions of this illusion: international research has shown that non-Western subjects, particularly those who are not regularly exposed to rectangular buildings and door frames, are less likely to misjudge the lines’ true lengths.

Paradox illusions encourage the mind to believe that it is seeing something known to be impossible. The Penrose Stairs and Penrose Triangle, developed by Lionel Penrose, are models created to illustrate this phenomenon. Naturally occurring optical illusions also exist. In various places around the world, objects appear to roll uphill, even though our knowledge tells us this is impossible. Visual information therefore conflicts with rational judgement. These locations, often called ‘gravity hills’ or ‘magnetic hills’, are popular with tourists. Their supposed mystical properties are vigorously promoted to add intrigue and are sometimes attributed to special magnetic properties of the land.

The scientific explanation is that these areas lie on slightly sloping ground without a visible horizon against which to establish perspective. Surrounding reference points that we expect to be perpendicular, such as trees, may themselves be on a slope. Observers’ interpretations are therefore confused: downward slopes may seem horizontal or tilted upwards, and cars with their handbrakes released appear to roll uphill when they are actually moving downhill under gravity. Our innate sense of balance normally helps us determine the ground’s inclination, but misleading visual stimuli and the lack of a horizon can override that ability, especially when the gradient is gentle.
